title: Which numbers can be written as a sum of numbers in a row?
description: Fifteen, nine and eight are each tried as a sum of numbers in a row, with two, three, four and five numbers laid out step by step. Fifteen and nine have ways, and eight has none. Keeko raises the doubt that four plus four makes eight work.
teaching_notes: One idea: numbers in a row each step up by one, so two of them always add to an odd number and a repeated number does not count. Watch for students who write a number twice, like four plus four, as a sum in a row.

source: Find every way to write 15 and 9 as a sum of consecutive nat
video_script.why: A learner sees that a number can be tested by trying rows of two, three, four and five numbers, and why some numbers have none.
video_script.substitution: the book's own numbers: fifteen, nine and eight
video_script.anchor: Ruhee writing numbers as sums of numbers in a row, as in the book
video_script.wrong_answer: eight can be written as four plus four
video_script.wrong_move: writes eight as four plus four, using the same number twice
video_script.payoff_line: Fifteen has three ways, nine has two ways, and eight has none.

final_answer.spoken: fifteen has three ways, nine has two ways, and eight has none

names.Ruhee: the child who explores sums of numbers in a row

maths_rules: four numbers from the start give 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, then 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 14, then 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 18, so fifteen is skipped
six numbers from the start give 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 + 6 = 21, which is above 15
9 = 4 + 5, 9 = 2 + 3 + 4; four numbers from the start give 10, above 9
two numbers in a row add to an odd number, and 8 is even
three numbers in a row add to 3 times the middle one; 8 divided by 3 is not whole
four numbers from the start give 10, above 8
video_script.design: One idea: try rows of two, three, four and five numbers and say why the others fail. Assumes natural numbers. Wrong idea: a repeated number counts as a row. The three ways for fifteen sit side by side so the count is visible.

beats.on_screen: title card Sum of Numbers in a Row; Ruhee sits with three number cards 15, 9 and 8 face up on the table

marks.scene: the title card arrives and Ruhee appears
marks.ask: the three cards 15, 9 and 8 slide onto the table

narration: <bookmark mark='scene'/>This is a question from your book about Ruhee and sums of numbers in a row.
<bookmark mark='ask'/>The book asks for every way to write fifteen and nine as such a sum.
Then it asks, can eight be written this way?

beats.on_screen: the three cards stay on the table while the child thinks

marks.think: Keeko sits at the corner of the board

narration: <bookmark mark='think'/>Think and tell.

beats.on_screen: a number line of cards 1 to 12 in a row; the pair 10, 11 and the trio 12, 13, 14 are bracketed; the word natural numbers is written under the line

marks.row: each card steps up by one as the cards line up
marks.pairs: the pair ten, eleven and the trio twelve, thirteen, fourteen are bracketed
marks.nat: the word natural numbers is written and the cards start at one

narration: <bookmark mark='row'/>Numbers in a row are numbers where each one is one more than the one before.
<bookmark mark='pairs'/>Ten and eleven are numbers in a row. Twelve, thirteen and fourteen are too.
<bookmark mark='nat'/>We use natural numbers here, which start from one.

beats.on_screen: Given: the numbers 15, 9 and 8, to be written as sums of numbers in a row
narration: <bookmark mark='given'/>Given, the numbers are fifteen, nine and eight, to be written as sums of numbers in a row.

beats.on_screen: To find: every way for 15 and 9; is there any way for 8?
narration: <bookmark mark='find'/>We have to find every way for fifteen and nine, and check eight.

beats.on_screen: 15: 7 + 8 = 15; 4 + 5 + 6 = 15; 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 + 5 = 15. Four numbers: 10, 14, 18 skip 15. Six numbers from 1 make 21

marks.two: the line seven plus eight is written
marks.three: four plus five plus six is written under it
marks.five: one to five is written, then the lines for four and six numbers are crossed out

narration: <bookmark mark='two'/>Step one, take fifteen. Two numbers work, since seven plus eight is fifteen.
<bookmark mark='three'/>Three numbers work, since four plus five plus six is fifteen. Five numbers work, since one to five adds to fifteen.
<bookmark mark='five'/>Four numbers add to ten, then fourteen, then eighteen, so they skip fifteen. Six numbers already make twenty one.

beats.on_screen: 9: 4 + 5 = 9; 2 + 3 + 4 = 9. Four numbers from 1 make 10, too big

marks.nine: the lines four plus five and two plus three plus four are written
marks.big: the four numbers line is crossed out

narration: <bookmark mark='nine'/>Step two, take nine. Four plus five is nine, and two plus three plus four is nine.
<bookmark mark='big'/>Four numbers start at ten, which is already too big. Nine has two ways.

beats.on_screen: 8, two numbers: odd + even = odd, never 8

marks.pair: two cards in a row, one odd and one even, light up
marks.odd: the sum is marked odd and 8 is marked even

narration: <bookmark mark='pair'/>Step three, take eight. Two numbers in a row are one odd and one even.
<bookmark mark='odd'/>Odd plus even is odd, but eight is even. Two numbers cannot work.

beats.on_screen: 8, three numbers: 3 × middle = 8, so middle = 8 ÷ 3, not whole. Four numbers: 1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10, too big

marks.three: three cards with their middle one lit; the middle is marked not whole
marks.four: one plus two plus three plus four shows ten, above eight

narration: <bookmark mark='three'/>Step four, three numbers in a row add to three times the middle one.
Eight divided by three is not a whole number, so three numbers fail.
<bookmark mark='four'/>Four numbers add to at least ten, which is above eight. No row of numbers works.
<bookmark mark='ans'/>Fifteen has three ways, nine has two ways, and eight has none.
Eight cannot be written as a sum of numbers in a row.

beats.on_screen: Keeko with a raised hand beside the cards
narration: <bookmark mark='hand'/>Keeko has raised a hand. Let us check the doubt and solve it.

beats.on_screen: Keeko's bubble shows 4 + 4 = 8; the two cards 4 and 4 sit side by side with no step between them; the bubble is struck through, then 4 + 5 = 9 appears

marks.doubt: the bubble with four plus four appears
marks.same: the two equal cards show no step between them
marks.fix: the bubble is struck through and four plus five shows nine

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks eight can be written as four plus four.
<bookmark mark='same'/>But four and four are the same number. Numbers in a row go up by one each time.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>The next number after four is five, and four plus five is nine, not eight.
